summary: An excerpt from a novel (Book 10, part 27) in which Lawrence, held in an interrogation room, uses sixteen years of mental discipline to calm his fear and despair about his situation. Randy, the interrogator, accuses him of running and questions him about his work with Securitat data-streams. Lawrence explains that he does signals intelligence, analyzing timing, frequency and length of data to spot anomalies, without needing to know the payload content.
one_line: Lawrence, under interrogation, calms his despair through mental discipline and explains his signals-intelligence work to Randy.
key_facts: Lawrence has spent sixteen years mastering his thoughts and uses that discipline to calm himself in the interrogation room.
Lawrence imagines his anxious thoughts as a streamer of mental ribbon that he lets slip through his mental fingers and sail away.
Randy enters the room carrying his own chair and tells Lawrence that innocent people don't run.
Lawrence calls Randy's claim a rather self-serving hypothesis.
Randy states that the interrogation in the room flows in one direction and is not a dialogue.
Randy asks Lawrence whether he works with Securitat data-streams.
Lawrence says he works with large amounts of data, including material from the Securitat, but it is rarely in cleartext.
Lawrence describes his work as sigint, meaning signals intelligence, analyzing the timing, frequency and length of different kinds of data to spot anomalies.
Lawrence notes that his analysis works best when he does not know what is in the payload of the data.
Lawrence compares this to a magician's trick, where the audience focuses on the rabbit or the glass of water and misses the method.
Lawrence's face hurts when he talks, but the pain fades when he thinks about what to say.
Randy observes that people who are uncomfortable tend to talk louder and lean forward a little.
